messages.subject_clean: Cairo device
messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I just installed Cairo-1.3-4, and the SVG export works just fine.
There's still no CairoSVG-device, although it has a help page. But it's
no problem to generate SVGs with the generic Cairo-device.

Thanks for fixing that!

Cheers,
Frederik



-- 
Frederik Elwert

Fachbereich Sozialwissenschaften

Richard,

On May 22, 2007, at 4:56 PM, Richard Percy wrote:

> Thanks Simon
>
> You guessed it: I'm trying to run an R source file from Java.  I  
> quickly discovered that it's best to use the source() function, as  
> you suggest.
>
> BTW I'm writing some wrappers so that the contributors to our  
> project can write R code files to do the difficult calcs instead of  
> Java.  R is just more accessible for most actuaries.  I inspect  
> return values from REngine.eval() and throw an exception if  
> appropriate.  The geterrmessage() function in R helps with the cause.
>
> Just wondered why you didn't build Java exceptions into JRI?

Simplicity and efficiency. There are engine-level exceptions, but at  
REXP level it assumes you know what you are doing and in that case  
they are superfluous (the justification for this is that the current  
API is very low-level, so you have to know what you're doing  
anyway ;)). Having to deal with unnecessary exceptions in Java is  
quite a pain. What is unnecessary is in the eye of the beholder,  
though ;).


>   Did you try it and encounter problems, or is this in the pipeline?
>

Yes, it is. There is a new API that I work on and it is shared both  
by Rserve and JRI, allowing you to switch between both back-ends. the  
Rserve part is ready, the JRI one I still work on. To have a look,  
you can either pull it off the SVN or fetch development snapshot of  
Rserve 0.5 (look in src/client/java-new) from http://www.rforge.net/ 
Rserve/


> One of your recent correspondents asked why you return zero if  
> someone tries to convert a non-int REXP to an int.  You replied  
> that Java doesn't have a nullable int.  Did you consider using the  
> class Integer instead of the builtin int?
>

That is highly inconvenient for several reasons: the whole point of  
having something like asInteger is to get the integer value, not an  
object. If you were happy with an object, just use asIntegerArray  
instead - that will return null if the result is not an integer and  
you can simply append [0] to get the integer value. Everything is  
stored internally as arrays, so there is no overhead.  However, using  
Integer just adds more overhead - a new object has to be created  
(which is slow in Java) and you are likely to call intValue() anyway  
thus it is unnecessary.

Please note that you should use asInteger only if you know that the  
result will be an integer (e.g. eval("as.integer(...)")) and in that  
case you don't care about any conversions. If the evaluation itself  
failed, then you will get an exception earlier anyway.

Cheers,
Simon

On May 31, 2007, at 6:13 PM, Lei Wu wrote:

> I'm trying to use JRI to replace my old code that uses Rserve now.  
> I wonder how JRI handle the consecutive request. For example, after  
> I issue a very time consuming R command through JRI, I issue second  
> command through JRI right after this. Is there any way that JRI or  
> JGR can remember the second command and execute it after the first  
> one finished? Or I should write my own queue to save all command?
>

I'm not quite sure what you mean - if you try to send a request while  
another one is processed, it will block until it is processed as  
well, so it is a kind of implicit queuing that you get. Clearly, only  
one eval will be inside R at each given time as R is not threaded  
(unless you use multiple JVMs ...).

Cheers,
Simon
